newsitem.title: UK: British galleries have art seized by Nazis - report.
newsitem.headline: British galleries have art seized by Nazis - report.

text.p: Some of the famous paintings on display in British art galleries were plundered by the Nazis in the years leading up to World War Two, a Sunday newspaper said.

The Sunday Times said that a list given to London's Victoria and Albert Museum by the widow of Swiss art dealer Harry Fischer has allowed historians to identify 10,000 paintings seized from Jews in Germany during the 1930s.
They include Edvard Munch's "The Sick Girl," which hangs in the Tate Gallery.

The list identifies works by Vincent van Gogh, Franz Marc and Paul Cezanne as being among those confiscated by top Nazi Hermann Goering and which "could be hidden anywhere from Paraguay to Peckham (in south London)," the Sunday Times quoted an expert as saying.

Adolf Hitler decided to cleanse Germany of the disturbing images by painters such as Pablo Picasso and Marc Chagall. The works were taken at first from Jewish collectors and put in museums but were later taken and burned in public.
With World War Two looming, the Nazis decided to sell thousands of the paintings and Fischer organised the auction in Switzerland in 1939.
London art dealers took a large share of the loot, but many British and Americans refused to bid on moral grounds, driving prices down, the Sunday Times said.
"The Sick Girl", given to the Tate by a Norwegian philanthropist in 1939, was sold for the equivalent of 47 pounds ($76) at today's prices. It is now worth several million dollars.

The United States, Britain and France are still trying to resolve the problem of millions of dollars of gold which the Nazis seized from Jews, most of which has been languishing in Swiss bank accounts since the war. ($1=.6161 Pound)
